passage:
Monday: Ojas sat on the step tugging at his shoelaces until they knotted. He threw the shoe. Bhavna Didi tied it for him.
Wednesday: He tried again with Didi's "bunny ears" rhyme. One loop flopped. He huffed, then made the loop again.
Saturday: Ojas bent down alone, whispered the rhyme and pulled tight. A bow! He jumped up, shoulders back, chin high, and marched into the kitchen. "Didi, look! I did it myself!" He walked in slow circles so everyone could see his feet.

qa.q: On which day did Ojas tie the bow by himself?
qa.a: He tied it by himself on Saturday.

qa.q: What does Ojas marching in with his chin high suggest?
qa.a: He felt proud of his own effort and wanted everyone to see what he had managed.

qa.q: How could Bhavna respond so his pride stays linked to effort?
qa.a: She could say, "You kept trying all week, and now you can do it!" so he connects the good feeling with practice. 🎉

qa.q: What would change if Bhavna had kept tying his shoes every day?
qa.a: Ojas would have missed the chance to succeed alone, and the proud Saturday moment would not have happened.

grounding: It shows a child standing tall with satisfaction after mastering a skill through his own effort.

passage: The water tanker came late, just as the light was fading, and the whole lane rushed out with buckets. Nirmala had two heavy ones and the baby on her hip. "I can take the small one, Amma," Uday said. He gripped the handle with both hands, walked slowly around the puddles, and set it down by their door without spilling. Nirmala looked in. "Full to the top!" Uday pushed out his chest, pulled his back very straight and went back to wait in the line.

qa.q: Why could Nirmala not carry everything herself?
qa.a: She had two heavy buckets and the baby on her hip.

qa.q: How can you tell Uday felt proud?
qa.a: After she praised the full bucket, he pushed out his chest, straightened his back and went back to the line.

qa.q: What small step could Nirmala take next to build on this?
qa.a: She could give him a small regular job, like carrying the little bucket each time, and notice how carefully he does it.

qa.q: How might Nirmala see Uday's help in that rushed moment?
qa.a: To her it was real help at a hard time, not a game, so her praise was likely warm and honest.

grounding: It shows a young child's pride and upright posture after succeeding at a real task under pressure.

passage: Kavitha pressed the crayon so hard it snapped, but the letters stood on the page: K-A-V-I-T-H-A, the V a little crooked. She held the paper up to the window of their flat in Pune so the light came through. Then she carried it to Santosh Mama, who was fixing the fan. "Read it," she said. He read it slowly, like a big announcement. Kavitha's feet did a little dance. She stuck the page on the fridge with a magnet and kept walking past it all afternoon.

qa.q: Where did Kavitha stick her page?
qa.a: She stuck it on the fridge with a magnet.

qa.q: Why did Kavitha keep walking past the fridge?
qa.a: She felt proud of writing her own name and seemed to enjoy seeing it again and again.

qa.q: How could Santosh Mama encourage her further?
qa.a: He could ask her to write his name next, or a label for the toolbox, so she gets to use her new skill.

qa.q: Why might Santosh Mama read the name "like a big announcement"?
qa.a: He seemed to understand how big this was for her and wanted to share in her pride.

grounding: It shows a child's satisfaction and delight after writing her name for the first time.

passage:
"Ammi, look! No hands on the seat!"
"Jaya! You're riding by yourself!" Parveen called.
Jaya wobbled, then pedalled to the gate and back. She hopped off and stood very straight, chin up.
"Did you see? All the way!"
"All the way. How does it feel?"
"Big!" Jaya patted the bike. "Tomorrow I'll show Abbu."
"He'll be so happy."
"I did it myself, na?"

qa.q: How far did Jaya ride on her own?
qa.a: She pedalled to the gate and back.

qa.q: What does Jaya standing very straight with her chin up suggest?
qa.a: It suggests she felt proud and satisfied after managing to ride by herself.

qa.q: Which part of Parveen's response helped Jaya's pride grow?
qa.a: She asked Jaya how it felt, letting her name her own good feeling instead of only praising her.

qa.q: How might Abbu feel when Jaya shows him tomorrow?
qa.a: He would probably feel happy and proud to see her new skill. 🎉

grounding: Illustrates a young child feeling satisfaction and standing taller after an achievement.

passage:
Teacher's note, Anjali Ma'am, UKG
Today Lalremsiami wrote her full name on her worksheet without looking at the name card. It is a long name! She held up the page and stood tall, cheeks pink, and walked around showing it to everyone. 😊 Later she offered to help a friend with her letters. I have pinned the page on the wall.

qa.q: What did Lalremsiami write without looking at the name card?
qa.a: She wrote her full name on her worksheet.

qa.q: How can you tell Lalremsiami felt proud?
qa.a: She stood tall with pink cheeks and walked around showing her page to everyone.

qa.q: Why was pinning the page on the wall a good choice?
qa.a: It honours her effort and keeps the achievement visible, which can encourage her to keep trying.

qa.q: How might the friend she helped see Lalremsiami after this?
qa.a: The friend may look up to her and feel encouraged to learn her own letters.

grounding: Shows a child's pride and taller posture after writing her long name, in a teacher's note.

passage: Every morning the milk can went from their house to the village dairy, and every morning Sarika carried it. Today her little brother Darshan, five, said, "I'll do it." Sarika walked beside him. He held the can with both hands, stopping twice to rest, and didn't spill a drop. At the dairy counter he lifted it up himself. On the way home he walked in front, chest out, waving at every neighbour.

qa.q: Who usually carried the milk can?
qa.a: Sarika carried it every morning.

qa.q: What does Darshan walking in front with his chest out suggest?
qa.a: He felt proud and grown-up after carrying the can all the way without spilling.

qa.q: How could Sarika help Darshan keep this good feeling?
qa.a: Let him carry the can again and tell the family what he managed, praising his effort.

qa.q: What is it like for Sarika to walk beside him instead of carrying the can?
qa.a: She may feel a bit anxious watching, but also glad and proud to see him manage.

grounding: Shows a young child standing taller with pride after carrying the milk can himself.

passage: In the park in Lyon, Amara, five, wobbled on her bike without the little side wheels. Her grandmother Ines jogged behind, holding the seat. "Let go? Don't let go!" Ines let go. Amara didn't notice for three long pedals. Then she did, squeaked, and kept going all the way to the fountain. She braked, turned round, and put both hands on her hips. "Grand-mère! I did it by myself!"

qa.q: Where did Amara ride to without help?
qa.a: All the way to the fountain.

qa.q: What does Amara putting both hands on her hips suggest?
qa.a: She felt proud and pleased with herself for riding alone.

qa.q: How could Ines respond to make the moment count?
qa.a: Celebrate the effort, like "you kept pedalling even when you noticed", not just the result.

qa.q: What was it like for Ines to let go of the seat?
qa.a: It was likely a nervous moment, followed by relief and joy when Amara kept going.

grounding: Shows a young child's pride after riding a bike alone for the first time.

passage: In the kindergarten, Seema, the class teacher, came round to look at the drawings. Shreya, five, had drawn her family under a big sun. At the bottom, in wobbly capital letters, she had written SHREYA. It was the first time she'd written her whole name without looking at the card. "Did you do this by yourself?" Seema asked. Shreya nodded, sat up very straight, and later asked to show it to the principal.

qa.q: What did Shreya write at the bottom of her drawing?
qa.a: She wrote SHREYA in wobbly capital letters.

qa.q: What does Shreya sitting up very straight suggest?
qa.a: She felt proud of writing her whole name by herself for the first time.

qa.q: How could Seema support Shreya's pride in this achievement?
qa.a: Let her take it to the principal and put it on the wall, praising the effort she put in.

qa.q: How might the principal see Shreya's visit?
qa.a: The principal would likely feel pleased and warm, seeing a small child so proud of her work.

grounding: Shows a young child's pride after writing her name alone for the first time.

passage: I'm Rafiq, and I live in the flat opposite Bidisha's. For two weeks I watched her fall off her small cycle in our compound, again and again, after her father took the side wheels off. She's five. Yesterday she pedalled all the way to the gate without falling. She stopped, put one foot down, and looked round to see who had seen. Then she walked the cycle back very slowly, chin up, shoulders back, like a queen. I clapped. She pretended not to care, but she was smiling.

qa.q: What did Bidisha's father take off her cycle?
qa.a: The side wheels.

qa.q: What might Bidisha have felt walking back with her chin up?
qa.a: Bidisha probably felt proud and satisfied after finally riding to the gate.

qa.q: How could adults support Bidisha's pride in her effort?
qa.a: Praise her practice and not giving up after falls, not just the result.

qa.q: How does Rafiq see Bidisha's success?
qa.a: Rafiq is pleased and amused, clapping and noticing she was smiling even while pretending not to care.

grounding: A neighbour watches a five-year-old stand taller with pride after learning to ride without side wheels.

passage:
Ten days before Ganesh Chaturthi, Pradeep, five, tried to shape a small clay Ganpati with his mother, Lakshmi. The trunk fell off. He squashed the whole thing and cried.
Five days later, he tried again, patting slowly. The ears were uneven, but the trunk stayed on.
On festival morning, his little Ganpati sat beside the big one on the altar. When his Mama visited, Pradeep stood very straight and said, "I made that one. By myself. Mostly."

qa.q: What fell off Pradeep's first clay Ganpati?
qa.a: The trunk.

qa.q: What does Pradeep standing very straight on festival morning show?
qa.a: Pradeep felt proud of making the Ganpati himself.

qa.q: How could Lakshmi encourage healthy pride?
qa.a: Praise his patience in trying again and his honest 'mostly', not just how it looks.

qa.q: How might Pradeep's Mama feel hearing 'By myself. Mostly'?
qa.a: Mama would likely feel charmed and amused by his pride and honesty.

grounding: Before Ganesh Chaturthi, a five-year-old moves from frustration to pride in his own clay idol.

passage: Sports day at Nilesh's school fell on the hottest April morning, and the sack race started late. Nilesh, six, had practised with a rice sack at home with his sister Kashish. Halfway, he tripped and fell flat. Other children passed him. He struggled up, hopped on, and crossed the line fourth, red-faced and dusty. He didn't win a medal. But when Kashish ran to him, he said, "I fell and I didn't stop!" and stood tall, holding the sack like a flag.

qa.q: Which place did Nilesh finish in?
qa.a: Fourth.

qa.q: How did Nilesh feel crossing the line fourth?
qa.a: Nilesh felt proud of himself for getting up and finishing, even without a medal.

qa.q: How could Kashish support Nilesh's pride?
qa.a: Praise his getting up and finishing, the part he is proudest of.

qa.q: How might Kashish feel seeing him stand tall with the sack?
qa.a: Kashish would likely feel proud and happy, having practised with him.

grounding: On a hot sports day, a six-year-old feels proud of finishing a race after falling.

passage:
On Christmas morning in their Bandra building, Elizabeth sat on the stairs and tried to tie her new shoes.

Loop. Around. Pull. It fell apart. She tried again.

On the fourth try, the bow held. She stood up, stamped her feet, and walked down the stairs very straight.

Rafiq Uncle from the ground floor looked up. "Who tied those?"

"Me," said Elizabeth, chin high. "All by myself."

qa.q: What did Elizabeth try to tie?
qa.a: She tried to tie her new shoes.

qa.q: How did Elizabeth feel when the bow held?
qa.a: Elizabeth felt proud, standing straight and saying she did it all by herself.

qa.q: How can adults support Elizabeth's pride in her new skill?
qa.a: Notice her effort and ask about it, as Rafiq Uncle did, so she feels her work is seen.

qa.q: How might Rafiq Uncle feel when Elizabeth said "All by myself"?
qa.a: Rafiq Uncle was probably amused and pleased by her proud answer.

grounding: On Christmas morning, a child feels proud after tying her shoes herself and stands taller.

passage:
"Ammi, look!" Irfan shouted. It was Eid morning, and he was on his cycle without the side wheels.

"Irfan! You're riding alone!" Jyoti said.

He pedalled to the gate and back. "I didn't fall even once!"

"You practised so much."

"I'm big now." He puffed out his chest.

"Very big. Will you ride to Nani's?"

"Tomorrow. Today I'm showing everyone."

qa.q: What did Irfan ride without?
qa.a: He rode his cycle without the side wheels.

qa.q: How did Irfan feel after riding to the gate and back?
qa.a: Irfan felt proud and grown-up, puffing out his chest.

qa.q: How did Jyoti support Irfan's pride?
qa.a: She praised his practice and asked about his next goal, not just the result.

qa.q: How might Jyoti feel watching Irfan ride alone?
qa.a: Jyoti was likely delighted and proud of him.

grounding: On Eid morning, a child proudly rides his cycle alone for the first time.

passage:
Kindergarten note, Diwali week.

We made Diwali cards today. Nandini has been practising her name for weeks. Today she wrote N-A-N-D-I-N-I on her card without looking at the chart.

She held the card up high and walked around the room showing everyone. Then she sat very straight in her chair.

I pinned her card on the board. — Shalini

qa.q: What did Nandini write on her card?
qa.a: She wrote N-A-N-D-I-N-I without looking at the chart.

qa.q: How did Nandini feel after writing her name?
qa.a: Nandini felt proud and satisfied, walking around to show everyone and sitting very straight.

qa.q: How did Shalini support Nandini's pride?
qa.a: She pinned Nandini's card on the board so her achievement was seen.

qa.q: How might the other children feel seeing Nandini's card?
qa.a: They might feel happy for her or want to try writing their own names.

grounding: A kindergarten note records a child's pride after writing her name alone on a Diwali card.

passage: On Pola morning in their village near Wardha, everyone was decorating the bullocks. For days Vasudha had tried to tie the brass bell on Shyam the bullock's neck rope, and each time the knot slipped. Today she pulled the ends tight, tugged, and the bell held. She stepped back, chin up, and rang it twice. "I did it myself!" Her cousin Bhupen looked over from painting the horns. "Not bad, Vasu." She walked Shyam to the gate so everyone passing could hear the bell.

qa.q: What had Vasudha tried to tie on Shyam's neck rope?
qa.a: She had tried to tie the brass bell.

qa.q: What does Vasudha walking to the gate suggest about how she feels?
qa.a: It suggests she feels proud of her knot and wants others to notice it.

qa.q: How could her family support her pride in a healthy way?
qa.a: They could notice her effort, like "You kept trying for days", rather than just calling her clever.

qa.q: How does Bhupen see Vasudha's achievement?
qa.a: Bhupen treats it lightly with "Not bad, Vasu", which sounds like a cousin's teasing but still approving.

grounding: Shows a young child standing taller with satisfaction after finally mastering a task during a village festival.
